title: CCH redesign: one running example
spec: prototypes/00-results.md (its Change list: proposed, not yet merged into 03)

conventions.ranks: Ranks are 1-based, as in 03 §2: pool ranks are 1..reserve. CSR rows are 0-based: row i holds rank i + 1.
conventions.weights: null in a weight array means +∞. null in a middle array means no middle.
conventions.arcs: An arc is (lo, hi) in rank space, lo < hi. Upward is node_of(lo) → node_of(hi); downward is the reverse.
conventions.matrices: Sparse matrices are lists of [row, col] or [row, col, value].
conventions.draw: Each step's draw names node and edge sets by role; edges are node-id pairs (space 'node') or rank pairs (space 'rank'); 'coarse:d:l' draws the fine graph with level-l groups of depth d.
conventions.work_units: Work units, as 03 §6b counts them: one per apex-merge step, one per heap push, one per seed lookup (each direction), plus S2's fixed costs: one per row entry the overlay reads and one per delta insert (Up and Down each).

notes: Node ids: 0–15 form the 4×4 grid (row-major, x = column, y = row); 16 and 17 hang off corner 15; 18 exists with no edge; 19 is a slot freed before the build. node_cap is 20 at the build; nodes created later take id 19 first (the engine hands out the lowest free id, graph/src/graph/id_space.rs:75) and then 20, 21, 22. Node 7 is deleted at v13, and its id is handed out again at v17.
A two-way road is two relationships, one per direction. So the pending deletion of road 2–7 is two dm entries and the pending addition of road 4–5 is two dp entries.

Added beyond the brief: ROAD 14→13 was replaced in one transaction (tensor state H: the old id stays in m with weight 1, the new id is in dp with weight 6). Without it the seed pass's ¬struct(dp) mask would remove nothing, and D1 would not show why it is there. The old weight is the smaller one on purpose: a pass that read the stale m value would then seed the dead, faster road, and the check in G can catch it (with a larger stale value, MIN would hide the bug).
FERRY has two relationships, both one-way: 10→9 (weight 2, parallel to ROAD 9–10 at 4) and 5→10 (weight 3, across the cell 5-6-9-10).
ROAD weights come from a fixed formula, 1 + (5·lo + 3·hi) mod 9 for the road lo–hi, so they are not random and the script can be re-run to the same numbers. Writers set their own weights.

Toy B_gil is 250 work units. Every writer commit fits except v14: its running total passes 250 at pop 15 of the recompute (257 units), and it stops there; finishing would have cost 506. The largest that fits is 201 units.

The 2-hop pass never fires on the running example: every matching shrinks its cell by at least 15 %, and the same holds for all 600 salt bases from 0 to 599 (B5.h re-runs the ordering under each). Forcing the trigger on every level pairs no vertex: the leftover vertices share an anchor only at depth 0 level 2 (vertices 3 and 0 under anchor 2), where the weight cap blocks the pair. So B5.h runs the same matching code on a side example, a star of 7 vertices, the shape that stalls mutual matching. It is not part of the running example's order.
The coarsest graph at depth 0 is complete (4 coarse vertices that all touch), so the first separator leaves one side empty. Node FM at the finer levels restores the balance (B7).

Decay signals (03 §6) are evaluated after every writer flush from v10 to v17 (at v14, on the writer's attempt before it hands off), with the toy thresholds in the Toy scale table. Met: S7's 'arcs ≥ 1.25 × arcs at build' from v12 on; S7's 'one commit adding > arcs/8' at v12 and v14; S7's 'top ranks ≥ reserve' from v12 on; S6's 'deletions ≥ n/8' from v13 on. The fold trigger is met from v12 to v16; the toy acts on it (the upkeep set at v12 and v15, and the fold published at v16). It does not act on S6 or S7. Under the design, the v12 writer would start S7, a re-order as a new generation through the batched build, with readers on the Dijkstra fallback, and the v14 commit would be S7 too. So the states after v12 show their rules on a hierarchy the design would already be replacing. The toy suppresses S6 and S7 so that the node delete, the hand-off, the fold and id reuse can be shown on one lineage; running the build once more would show nothing new.

bound.text: If a copy's unconsumed pairs pass max(1M pairs, arcs/8), the writer replaces that copy's whole unconsumed list with one Overflow{seq = its version} node, and resets pairs to 0. An Overflow node is relinked, consumed and freed exactly like a segment. The phase that consumes an Overflow rescans.
bound.built: An Overflow is never created on a Built entry. Past the §5 bound, the writer clears upkeep and the log instead of writing an Overflow: the job is abandoned, and a later commit re-triggers it.

rows: Relink the fork's own nodes (seq = fork.version, above every published seq) onto the published log. An own Overflow is relinked like a segment.

Run the §6 flush over the own nodes, resolved against the fork graph, onto the published hierarchy, within the remaining B_gil. Over budget, or an own Overflow: Absorbed::Restart, which takes next_generation(), with Building{Repair, base = the published hierarchy, log = the own nodes}.
Fold: re-apply the fold to the fork's copy. S6: replay the own nodes through §6 onto the new lineage, within B_gil; over budget, Restart as above.
Unreachable: a Built entry becomes Building only through a writer's commit (a hand-off or S7, both new generations), which makes this fork stale.
rebase.note: A writer always keeps its own nodes in its private version until it publishes, whatever the entry state, so every row above has them.

hooks.why: The log is in CchIndex's own per-version state. CCH contributes no ids to the framework's Written, so since_last_indexer_step stays empty for CCH, and indexer_apply's clear never touches it.

fold.overtaken: At its publish the fold clears upkeep and the log, and counts the publish in the entry's indexer_commits, so writers forked before it are overtaken. A writer that overtook a fold applies the same function to its own copy: its bases become the folded ones, and its deltas become the arcs of its own added_since_fold with seq > F. No segment is replayed, because no value changes.
fold.retention: Without retention, a fold needs no log: metric-only writes after F stay in the published metric, which the fold keeps. Retention serves S6, which replays the retained nodes with seq > F onto the new lineage.

items: Ranks are lazy: isolated nodes and unused ids get no rank. A rank-less node has no indexed edge at that version (I1′).

A rank-less node with a live edge takes the lowest free pool rank if its degree is ≤ 1 and free_ranks is not empty; otherwise it takes the next top rank n_r′ + 1. After the build that rank lives only in the deltas; at Supergraph it raises the base's dimension, since nothing lives in a delta yet (03 §4 step 1).
Allocation is a phase of its own, run before classification by every resolver: writer flush, Supergraph, Seal, Repair, the Overflow paths and S6.

A pool rank never has a holder (P: r ∈ free_ranks ⇔ node_of[r] = None), so taking one never strips a node. Within a lineage a rank never goes back to the pool: deleted nodes keep their rank; only S6 and S7 rebuild the pool.

rank_of is partial and injective. Readers: the query's endpoint lookup, which answers “no path” unless source = target; and partial.rs:115-118, which must check for the rank's presence as well as the bound.

up_ids(r) yields ascending (hi, id) pairs from merging base and delta; arrays are sized by arc_capacity. Readers: relax's x_slots_start + i (customize.rs:497-513), query.rs:113, partial.rs:151,170 (the heap carries (lo, hi, id)), Cch::joins, and the full-seed pass and the fold, which write by id.
contracts.why_delta: Why a base plus a delta, not VersionedMatrix: VersionedMatrix decides folds itself (its next flush runs an O(|m|) eWiseAdd on the writer, under the lock), its set exists only for bool, and a GraphBLAS delta read while it is written pays pending-tuple assembly. A cow_btree insert costs O(log n), has no pending tuples, and can hold ranks above the base's dimension, so the base is never resized.
contracts.why_arrays: Why the base exposes raw arrays: relax opens up(y) once per arc and steps once per triangle, and a re-seeked GraphBLAS row iterator costs ≈298 instructions per seek (≈1.7G in seeks alone on California, derived). So queries and customization read the base as flat slices, and GraphBLAS reads the same memory through a read-only load for its algebra (decision D3).
contracts.source: 03 §2 Contract changes; Why base plus delta; Why the base exposes raw arrays

design_questions.question: §2 defines n_r = ranked + reserve, with ranked counting nodes with an edge in the skeleton or the log at V_sg; that gives 22 here. §3 step 0 ranks only the skeleton's nodes and §4 step 1 ranks the log's nodes at Supergraph, which gives n_r = 20 and n_r′ = 21. The toy follows §3 and §4.

§6 says that while upkeep is set every writer keeps its nodes; §7 says a Built entry with upkeep = Some{since} keeps its nodes with seq > since. The writer that sets upkeep has seq = since, so the two differ on that writer's node. The toy follows §7 (the job forks at F ≥ since and needs only seq > F).

'The writer whose flush crosses a trigger sets upkeep' does not say what a writer does when the trigger is already met and no upkeep is set, as after a hand-off discards the job. §6 Retention says that after an abandoned job 'a later commit re-triggers it'. The toy reads both as: a writer whose flush ends with the trigger met and no upkeep sets it (v12 and v15).

The S6 signal's n and 'dead ids' are not defined, and 'arcs' in 'one commit adding > arcs/8' could be the count before or after the commit. The toy uses n = the rank dimension, the count before the commit, and does not evaluate dead ids.

§2 lists 'top ranks used' among LineageStats' counters, and §6's S7 signal reads 'top ranks ≥ reserve'. Neither says whether a top rank given at build time counts. Supergraph (§4 step 1) gives node 20 top rank 21 at v7. The toy counts it: 'top ranks used' is 1 at the build, so the signal (2 ≥ reserve 2) is met at v12, when one more top rank is taken. If build-time top ranks did not count, it would read 1 there and not be met (SIMPLIFICATIONS #41).
